title: IFT-BioSim
text:
IFT-BioSim asks how a common national transition objective can create very different economic pressures across heterogeneous farms.
It focuses on who bears adjustment, who responds, and how policy design changes incidence.

title: IFT-BioSim
IFT-BioSim
text:
Why it matters
A technically feasible national pathway does not reveal how costly the transition may be for particular farms. IFT-BioSim is designed to make that distribution visible and to test whether alternative compensation or incentive designs change the burden.

title: BioLand-US
text:
BioLand-US asks a practical implementation question:

When a techno-economic model allocates land to perennial biomass, how much of that prospective allocation can also be supported by compatible agricultural land and voluntary contractual participation?

The model does not replace or re-optimise the upstream resource allocation. It adds an explicit implementation layer.

title: BioLand-US

BioLand-US asks a practical implementation question:

title: BioLand-US
text:
Scientific logic
The framework keeps four quantities distinct:
Techno-economic biomass allocation
        ↓
Compatible agricultural land
        ↓
Contractually accessible land
        ↓
Prospectively mobilised biomass
This makes it possible to distinguish technical allocation from land compatibility and actual access through voluntary contracts.

title: E-SEAT
text:
E-SEAT studies the relationship between fuel-market reform and structural land-use persistence in the U.S. Corn Belt.
Its central question is:

If the ethanol-demand signal weakens, how much of current Corn Belt specialisation is likely to reverse, and how much reflects the production structure already in place?

title: E-SEAT
text:
E-SEAT studies the relationship between fuel-market reform and structural land-use persistence in the U.S. Corn Belt.
Its central question is:

If the ethanol-demand signal weakens, how much of current Corn Belt specialisation is likely to reverse, and how much reflects the production structure already in place?

title: E-SEAT
text:
Design
The framework links county-level agricultural data, national corn-ethanol demand, predetermined county conditions, fixed-effects estimation, dynamic analysis, scenario translation, backcasting and spatial diagnostics.
The empirical structure covers counties across the Corn Belt over repeated Census of Agriculture waves from 1997 to 2022.

title: E-SEAT
text:
Main distinction
The analysis separates responsiveness from starting position.
A county may respond to a weaker ethanol-demand signal and still remain highly specialised because it begins from a very different agricultural structure.

title: E-SEAT
text:
Workflow
Source data
    ↓
County panel
    ↓
Fixed-effects estimation
    ↓
County sensitivity
    ↓
Scenario translation and backcast
    ↓
Persistence diagnostics
    ↓
Spatial interpretation

title: E-SEAT
text:
Reproducibility
Stata is used for data preparation, estimation, scenario translation and frozen county outputs. Python is used for publication cartography.
The public replication archive will be linked here once the full manuscript-facing release is complete.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
National AFOLU pathways can specify how livestock numbers, land release and future land uses change without showing where those changes fall.
GOBLIN-Spatial asks:

When a nationally coherent agricultural transition requires restructuring, where does transition pressure concentrate, what can the released land support, and can competing future land-use requirements be accommodated within the available geography?

GOBLIN supplies the national pathway. GOBLIN-Spatial resolves its geography and tests spatial feasibility.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
National AFOLU pathways can specify how livestock numbers, land release and future land uses change without showing where those changes fall.
GOBLIN-Spatial asks:

When a nationally coherent agricultural transition requires restructuring, where does transition pressure concentrate, what can the released land support, and can competing future land-use requirements be accommodated within the available geography?

GOBLIN supplies the national pathway. GOBLIN-Spatial resolves its geography and tests spatial feasibility.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
How it works
National GOBLIN pathway
        ↓
Transition incidence
Where does adjustment fall?
        ↓
Spatial response potential
What can released land support?
        ↓
Spatial transformability
Can competing future land uses fit?
        ↓
Spatial flexibility
Is one geography necessary?
The framework is a spatial stress-test of transition pathways, not a prediction of individual farmer or parcel decisions.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Evidence and scale
The historical reconstruction covers 2015–2025 and is anchored to the 2020 Census of Agriculture at Electoral Division level. Higher-level livestock controls maintain national accounting consistency while preserving validated local structure.
The model combines agricultural statistics with land, soil and drainage information, LPIS context and explicit eligibility controls.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
What it does not claim
The model does not predict individual farmer behaviour, household welfare, market prices, parcel-level adoption or the exact geography that will exist in 2050.
Those questions require behavioural, farm-level or market models.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Research context
GOBLIN-Spatial is being developed at the University of Galway within the wider GOBLIN modelling framework and the FUSION/FORESIGHT research environment.
My doctoral research is supervised by David Styles and Cathal O’Donoghue.

title: Research
text:
My research asks a distributional question:
National pathways are useful, but they can conceal very different local realities. Two regions can contribute to the same national target while facing different production structures, land constraints, opportunity costs and feasible alternatives.
I therefore work across scales. National pathway models define the transition. Spatial models show where it falls. Farm-level and behavioural models examine how heterogeneous producers may respond.

title: Research
text:
Current strands

Agricultural and land-use transitions
I study livestock restructuring, land release, afforestation, wetland rehabilitation, bioenergy and other AFOLU transitions, with particular attention to how nationally coherent pathways translate into local exposure and land-use opportunity.


Spatial incidence and feasibility
Through GOBLIN-Spatial, I examine where agricultural adjustment occurs, what the resulting transition space can support, and whether competing future land uses can fit within finite eligible land.


Farm and behavioural response
Farm-level work examines opportunity costs, participation, income effects and alternative policy designs. The purpose is to distinguish technical potential from economically and behaviourally accessible change.


Bioenergy and resource mobilisation
My U.S. work asks similar implementation questions in a different setting: how much prospective biomass remains plausible after land compatibility, contractual access and existing production structure are made explicit.

title: Research
text:
Methods
I use econometrics, spatial modelling, optimisation, synthetic populations and microsimulation, with Python, R, Stata, GIS and SQL as implementation tools.
The methods are secondary to the research question. Their role is to connect national objectives with the farms, land and places through which those objectives must be implemented.

title: Why I’m Excited to Work with FUSION and FORESIGHT
text:
FORESIGHT project illustration. Source: FUSION, University of Galway.


One of the most exciting parts of my PhD journey has been working in the FUSION research environment at the University of Galway and contributing to research connected with FORESIGHT.
FUSION stands for FUture Sustainable economy Integrated mOdelling Network. What attracts me to the group is that it does not treat sustainability as a problem that belongs to one discipline. Its work brings together life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment modelling, land-use analysis and environmental software engineering. The common thread is the use of quantitative models to ask practical questions about how economies, food systems and landscapes could change in the future.
That way of thinking fits naturally with the questions that interest me.
Agriculture and land use are full of difficult trade-offs. A national climate target can look clear on paper, but implementation happens through real production systems, farms, forests and communities. A pathway that appears technically feasible at national scale may look very different once land availability, livestock systems, economic incentives, spatial variation and alternative uses of land are considered.
This is where FORESIGHT, or Future ORiEnted ScenarIo modellinG of Holistic land use sTrategies, becomes especially interesting. The project provides agriculture and land-use modelling evidence for Ireland and continues the development of integrated AFOLU modelling tools such as GOBLIN. Its emphasis is not simply on predicting one future. It is about exploring plausible pathways, testing assumptions and understanding what different choices could mean for emissions, land use, resilience and wider sustainability objectives.
For me, that distinction matters. Forecasting asks what is likely to happen. Foresight asks a broader question: what futures are possible, what would be required to reach them, and what might we learn by working backwards from those outcomes?
My own work increasingly sits in that space. I am interested in taking national agricultural and land-use pathways and resolving them into more detailed spatial and farm-level questions. Where does adjustment occur? Which production systems are most exposed? What alternatives are actually feasible in particular places? How do economic and behavioural responses change the picture? And how can models become reusable decision-support tools rather than one-off academic exercises?
Working alongside researchers developing GOBLIN and related modelling approaches has reinforced something I increasingly value in research: the model itself is not the final product. The useful output is better evidence for a difficult decision.
That is what makes FUSION and FORESIGHT exciting to me. They create a space where environmental science, economics, modelling and software can meet around real policy problems, while keeping the analytical work transparent and open to improvement.
I expect many posts on this site will grow from that environment. Some will explain models and methods. Others will discuss new papers, data, land-use questions, agriculture, bioenergy or interesting developments in Ireland, the United States and elsewhere.
The aim is simple: use the blog as a place to think in public, connect research to current questions, and make technical work easier to understand.

title: About
text:
I am a PhD Researcher and Research Assistant in Plant & AgriBiosciences at the University of Galway’s Ryan Institute.
My research asks how national agricultural, climate and land-use objectives translate into different costs, opportunities and constraints across farms, production systems and places.

title: About
text:
Research
My current work combines spatial, economic and behavioural modelling of agricultural and land-use transitions.
The main projects are GOBLIN-Spatial, BioLand-US, E-SEAT and IFT-BioSim.
